units.translation: c. Nor did he revere him even a little: he paid not the slightest heed to Zeus himself, revealing divine thoughts to all. For by telling all his mind to men, he left them no need of the gods. That Phineus ruled all the Thracians in Asia as far as the Bosporus—these are the Bithynians and Paphlagonians—Pherecydes says in the sixth book (3 F 27 J.). Hesiod says in the Great Ehoiai (fr. 151 Rz.²) that Phineus was blinded because he revealed the way to Phrixus, and in the third book of the Catalogues (fr. 52 Rz.²), because he preferred long life to sight. They say his sons were Mariandynus and Thynus, and from Thynus the land was called Thynia, and from Mariandynus Mariandynia.
185. ὀνείασιν: with foods, with meats. Lg (P)
192. μὴ καὶ λευκανίην γ〈ε〉: some say the part hanging from the uvula, but Amerias says the throat and the windpipe.
b. ὧν οἱ ἰόντων: of which, when they came, it was fated for him by Zeus to have enjoyment of the foods that he would take.
197. ἀκήριον: like a lifeless little dream, because he was wasted away by the disease.
200-01a. πίνῳ τέ οἱ: and his skin, dried up, was befouled with filth.
b. The skin alone held the bones together inside. Lg
203-04. κάρος: a stupor seized him, that is, a darkening of sight. He thought the earth was moving because of his dizziness, as if he said that he thought the earth was pressing upon him.

205. ἀβληχρῷ: with weakening or weak, by privation of βληχρός. The sense: by that slight downward pull due to the darkening he lay speechless. κώματι means sleep, collapse; and it is by syncope from κοίμημα—as οἴμημα gives οἶμα and δόμημα gives δῶμα—and by change of the diphthong οι to ω, κῶμα.
206-08a. περισταδόν: instead of they stood around, having gathered about him. And they were astonished instead of they were struck with amazement.

b. ἐξ ὑπάτοιο στήϑεος: as if from the top and not from the depth, being unable to breathe and speak because of weakness. The word μόλις hints at nothing other than the violence and greatness of the disease.

Whom Phineus had married after divorcing Cleopatra; and she had become an old woman accuser of Phineus before Heracles. Therefore Heracles, finding the sons innocent, brought them back to their father's house, and when Phineus rose up and wanted to drown one of the sons, Heracles kicked him and killed him. Istrus (fr. 60a M. I 426) says that Aeetes, learning that he had saved the sons of Phrixus by his prophecies, cursed him, and Helius heard and blinded him.
